raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic heart failure syndrome with left ventricular systolic dysfunction that presents toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, after exclusion of alternative causes such as pre-existing cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, myocarditis, sepsis, or hypertensive pulmonary edema [1], [2]. Contemporary position statements generally use a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <45% as the echocardiographic threshold, although the ventricle need not be dilated [3]. PPCM is clinically important because it affects otherwise young women, can mimic normal late-pregnancy dyspnea and edema, and has outcomes ranging from full recovery to refractory heart failure, arrhythmia, thromboembolism, mechanical circulatory support, transplantation, or death [4], [5].

Epidemiology varies strikingly by geography and ascertainment. Estimates in the United States are near 1 in 2,000–3,000 births, with increasing reported incidence, whereas much higher burdens occur in parts of Africa and Haiti [6], [7]. Administrative US data suggest rising diagnoses over time and higher risk among Black women, older mothers, those with hypertension or pre-eclampsia, and multifetal gestation [8]. The Nigerian PEACE registry illustrates regional clustering and the importance of local context, including marked geographic heterogeneity within one country [9]. In the global ESC EORP registry, patients were enrolled across 49 countries; two-thirds had NYHA III/IV symptoms and two-thirds had LVEF ≤35% at diagnosis, underscoring frequent late recognition [10]. The North American IPAC study, by contrast, showed substantial recovery in many women but persistent cardiomyopathy or major adverse events in a clinically important minority [11]. Nigerian outcome data also demonstrate that mortality and recovery differ substantially by setting and access to guideline-directed therapy [12].

Pathogenesis is best conceptualized as a “two-hit” syndrome: pregnancy-related vascular, hormonal, inflammatory, and metabolic stress superimposed on susceptible myocardium [13], [14]. A seminal STAT3-deficient mouse model linked oxidative stress, cathepsin-D cleavage of prolactin, and a cardiotoxic 16-kDa prolactin fragment to postpartum cardiomyopathy [13]. A complementary angiogenic model implicated soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt1), impaired VEGF signaling, and inadequate cardiac proangiogenic reserve, providing a mechanistic bridge between PPCM, pre-eclampsia, and multifetal gestation [14]. MicroRNA-146a has been identified as a downstream mediator and potential biomarker of prolactin-fragment injury [15]. Genetics is also central: truncating variants, especially in TTN, occur in a meaningful subset and overlap with dilated cardiomyopathy genetics [16]. Larger sequencing studies confirm a heterogeneous genetic landscape and support consideration of genetic counseling/testing, particularly with severe disease, family history, arrhythmias, or incomplete recovery [17]. Inflammation may modify phenotype and prognosis; elevated inflammatory markers and Fas/Apo-1 have been associated with worse outcomes [18], while IPAC biomarker analyses support roles for sFlt1 and other vascular-hormonal pathways [19].

Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion. Persistent orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, pulmonary edema, marked tachycardia, hypoxemia, elevated natriuretic peptides, cardiomegaly, or new murmurs should prompt electrocardiography and urgent echocardiography [3], [20]. Early diagnosis matters: women diagnosed earlier postpartum have higher likelihood of recovery, partly because advanced remodeling and treatment delay are avoided [20]. Cardiac magnetic resonance can help characterize myocarditis, infarction, Takotsubo syndrome, scar, thrombus, and ventricular volumes, but echocardiography remains the practical diagnostic cornerstone.

Management is multidisciplinary and depends on pregnancy status, lactation, hemodynamics, fetal status, and severity. Acute pulmonary edema is treated with oxygen, cautious diuresis, vasodilators when appropriate, and intensive care for shock; severe cases require cardio-obstetric, anesthesia, critical-care, and advanced-heart-failure input, with consideration of inotropes, vasopressors, temporary mechanical circulatory support, and individualized delivery planning [21]. Postpartum HFrEF therapy generally includes beta-blockers, renin-angiotensin system inhibition, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and diuretics; during pregnancy, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, ARNIs, MRAs, and SGLT2 inhibitors are generally avoided, while hydralazine/nitrates, beta-blockers, and diuretics are used selectively [3], [21]. Anticoagulation is considered for very low LVEF, intracardiac thrombus, atrial fibrillation, or bromocriptine exposure, given the hypercoagulable peripartum state.

Bromocriptine, a dopamine agonist that suppresses prolactin release, is the main disease-specific therapy studied. A small randomized South African pilot suggested improved LVEF and clinical outcomes [22]; a German multicenter trial found high recovery and low event rates with short- or longer-course bromocriptine added to standard therapy, although no placebo group was included [23]. Meta-analytic data remain encouraging but limited by small, heterogeneous studies; when used, bromocriptine requires lactation suppression and thromboprophylaxis [24]. Immune phenotyping studies emphasize biologic heterogeneity and the need for targeted rather than uniform adjunctive strategies [25].

Follow-up should continue until sustained recovery and often beyond, because incomplete recovery predicts relapse and adverse outcomes. Subsequent pregnancy is a major counseling issue: recurrence and deterioration can occur even after apparent recovery, and risks are highest when LVEF remains abnormal [26]. Recent meta-analyses confirm substantial relapse risk and support preconception assessment, shared decision-making, contraception counseling, and close cardio-obstetric surveillance when pregnancy proceeds [27], [30]. Systematic reviews of outcomes show that approximately half of women recover normal LVEF, but death, persistent dysfunction, thromboembolism, arrhythmias, and neonatal complications remain important [28], [29]. Future priorities include earlier detection algorithms, equitable cardio-obstetric access, genotype- and biomarker-guided risk stratification, and adequately powered trials of prolactin blockade and modern heart failure therapies.
